title: Given a Scenario, Monitor Suspicious Activities to Identify Common Attacks

sections.title: What You Are Learning
paragraphs: Cloud defenders need to recognize when normal activity becomes suspicious.
CompTIA wants you to examine events, changes from normal behavior, exposed services, and signs of common attacks.
The core mental model is: know normal → identify abnormal → connect the symptom to the attack.

sections.title: Maestro Focus
paragraphs: What changed from normal behavior, and which attack best explains that change?
sections.callout: Unexpected activity + unusual resource usage + exposed service + suspicious user behavior → investigate the likely attack.

sections.title: Event Monitoring
paragraphs: Event monitoring reviews system, application, network, and security activity for suspicious behavior.
Events may reveal failed logins, configuration changes, unusual network activity, new processes, and resource spikes.
Think: Watch what the environment is doing.
sections.callout: Suspicious behavior must be detected from recorded system activity → event monitoring.

sections.title: Deviation from the Baseline
paragraphs: A baseline represents normal behavior. A deviation occurs when activity moves significantly away from what is normally expected.
Examples include CPU normally at 20% suddenly reaching 100%, a normal login pattern changing to several countries, or typical network volume suddenly multiplying.
Think: You cannot recognize weird until you know normal.
sections.callout: Behavior differs sharply from established normal activity → deviation from the baseline.

sections.title: Unnecessary Open Ports
paragraphs: Every open port can create another potential entry point. Services that are not needed should not remain exposed.
Think: An open door with nobody using the room should be closed.
sections.callout: An unused service is reachable from the network → unnecessary open port.

sections.title: Attack Types: Vulnerability Exploitation
paragraphs: Vulnerability exploitation occurs when attackers take advantage of weaknesses in software, configuration, or systems.

entries.title: Human Error
paragraphs: A user or administrator may accidentally create a vulnerability through misconfiguration, incorrect permissions, or exposure of resources.
Think: Not every security hole was intentionally created.
entries.recognitionCue: An accidental configuration exposes a system → human error.

entries.title: Outdated Software
paragraphs: Software that has not been patched may contain known exploitable vulnerabilities.
Think: Old software can mean old holes attackers already know about.
entries.recognitionCue: Attackers exploit a known flaw that should have been patched → outdated software.

sections.title: Social Engineering
paragraphs: Social engineering attacks humans instead of directly attacking technology.

entries.title: Phishing
paragraphs: Phishing uses deceptive messages or websites to persuade victims to reveal information or perform harmful actions.
Attackers may attempt to steal passwords, authentication tokens, or financial information.
Think: Trick the person to open the door.
entries.recognitionCue: A fraudulent message tries to steal credentials → phishing.

sections.title: Malware
paragraphs: Malware is malicious software designed to harm, control, disrupt, or misuse systems.
sections.callout: An unknown malicious program is running on a cloud workload → malware.

sections.title: Ransomware
paragraphs: Ransomware is malware that denies access to data or systems, often by encrypting information and demanding payment.
Think: Your data is locked, and the attacker wants a ransom.
sections.callout: Files suddenly become encrypted and payment is demanded → ransomware.

sections.title: Distributed Denial-of-Service (DDoS)
paragraphs: A DDoS attack uses many systems to overwhelm a target with traffic or requests. The goal is usually to make the service unavailable.
Think: Too much traffic from too many places.
sections.callout: A cloud service becomes unavailable because of massive distributed traffic → DDoS.

sections.title: Cryptojacking
paragraphs: Cryptojacking occurs when attackers secretly use another organization's computing resources to perform cryptocurrency mining.
Cloud environments are attractive targets because compute resources can be consumed quickly. Signs can include unexpected CPU usage, unexpected resource creation, and an increased cloud bill.
Think: Somebody is using your cloud horsepower to make themselves money.
sections.callout: Unexplained compute usage and billing spikes appear from cryptocurrency mining → cryptojacking.

sections.title: Zombie Instances
paragraphs: A zombie instance is a cloud resource that continues running even though it is no longer actively needed or properly managed.
It can waste money, remain unpatched, become forgotten, and increase the attack surface.
Think: Dead to the business, still alive in the cloud.
sections.callout: An abandoned virtual machine is still running unnoticed → zombie instance.

sections.title: Metadata
paragraphs: Cloud instances may have access to metadata containing information about the instance and its environment.
If improperly protected or accessed by an attacker, metadata may reveal sensitive information or credentials.
Think: Information about a cloud resource can itself become valuable to an attacker.
sections.callout: An attacker attempts to retrieve instance information or credentials from cloud metadata → metadata attack.

sections.title: Attack Recognition Cues
bullets: Review suspicious events → Event monitoring
Activity differs from normal → Deviation from the baseline
Unused network service is exposed → Unnecessary open port
An attacker uses a weakness → Vulnerability exploitation
A misconfiguration creates a weakness → Human error
A known unpatched vulnerability is exploited → Outdated software
A fake login email appears → Phishing
A malicious program runs → Malware
Files are encrypted and a ransom is demanded → Ransomware
Massive distributed traffic appears → DDoS
Unexpected cryptocurrency mining occurs → Cryptojacking
A forgotten cloud resource is still running → Zombie instance
An attacker retrieves instance identity or configuration information → Metadata

entries.title: DDoS vs. Cryptojacking
paragraphs: Both can cause heavy resource usage. Ask why the resources are busy.
Huge incoming traffic suggests DDoS. Unauthorized compute performing cryptocurrency mining suggests cryptojacking.

entries.title: Malware vs. Ransomware
paragraphs: Ransomware is a specific type of malware. If the defining symptom is encryption plus a payment demand, choose ransomware.

entries.title: Zombie Instance vs. Compromised Instance
paragraphs: A zombie instance may simply be forgotten and unmanaged. That does not automatically mean it has been compromised.
Abandoned resources can still become security risks because nobody is maintaining them.

entries.title: Human Error vs. Attack
paragraphs: Human error can create the vulnerability, and an attacker can then exploit that weakness.
An administrator accidentally exposing storage is human error. An attacker downloading that exposed data is exploitation.

entries.title: Baseline Deviation vs. Attack
paragraphs: A baseline deviation is an indicator, not automatic proof of an attack. Investigate what caused the abnormal behavior.

bullets: Watch suspicious system activity → Event monitoring
Activity differs from normal → Baseline deviation
Unused service is exposed → Unnecessary open port
Attacker uses a weakness → Vulnerability exploitation
Administrator accidentally exposes a resource → Human error
Old unpatched vulnerability is exploited → Outdated software
Fake message steals credentials → Phishing
Malicious program → Malware

Distributed traffic overwhelms service → DDoS
Unauthorized cryptocurrency mining → Cryptojacking
Forgotten cloud resource still running → Zombie instance
Attacker targets instance information or credentials → Metadata

Know normal first → Detect abnormal
